To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
event-driven simulations of large networks of spiking integrate-and-fire neurons with dynamic synapses are feasible and efficient.

event-driven simulation of large recurrent networks of spiking integrate-and-fire neurons is possible, and that the computational load per spiking neuron is about 6 times that of conventional simulation, and is only slightly larger than the load per nonspiking neuron.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an algorithm that is able to simulate large networks of spiking and dynamically plastic neurons.
the design of efficient simulation algorithms for recurrent neural networks of integrate-and-fire neurons, with spike-driven dynamics of synaptic efficacies and spike-driven synaptic plasticity.

the design of efficient simulation algorithms for large-scale neural networks, which are based on the dynamics of the neurons and the synapses, rather than on the dynamics of a neural network as a whole.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the event-driven algorithm is a viable and promising alternative for the simulation of recurrent neural networks with dynamic synapses.
event-driven simulation provides a very efficient way to simulate large recurrent networks of integrate-and-fire neurons with plastic synapses.
the event-driven simulation procedure described here is a powerful and efficient method of simulating large networks of neurons and synapses with spike-driven dynamics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
event-driven simulation of large networks of spiking, dynamical neurons and plastic synapse is feasible and efficient.
we have developed an efficient algorithm that makes feasible simulations with large numbers of neurons and synapses, which are dynamically changing as a function of neural activity.
the event-driven approach makes feasible the simulation of networks of neurons with dynamic synapses, and thus allows the exploration of the rich dynamics of recurrent neural networks.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the computational load of large-scale recurrent neural networks can be kept at a manageable level, even in the presence of dynamical synapses, if the dynamics are event-driven.
it is feasible to perform simulations of recurrent neural systems with dynamic synapses, and that such simulations can be made very efficient.

it is possible to perform large-scale simulations of networks of spiking and dynamical neurons, with realistic spike-driven synaptic dynamics, in a way that is computationally efficient, and that can be easily implemented in hardware.
